Modeling Equivalent Fractions: 1. 6 parts, 3 shaded: 1/2 = 3/6. 2. 6/8. 3. 8; multiply both by 4. 4. Split each fourth into 3 equal pieces: there are 12 pieces, and the shaded fourth is now 3 of them, so 1/4 = (1 × 3)/(4 × 3) = 3/12. 5. Yes: 1/3 = (1 × 2)/(3 × 2) = 2/6. 6. 6.
Fraction Strips: 1. Examples: 2/6, 3/9, 4/12. 2. Yes: 3/4 = (3 × 2)/(4 × 2) = 6/8; the 3/4 strip and 6/8 strip line up. 3. 4.
Which Is Greater?: 1. 3/8 < 1/2, because 1/2 = 4/8. 2. 5/6 > 5/8: both have 5 pieces, and sixths are bigger than eighths. 3. 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so 2/3 < 3/4. 4. 3/5 = 6/10, so 7/10 > 3/5. 5. Kai: 4/5 = 8/10, and 8/10 > 7/10. 6. 1/4 (3/12), 1/3 (4/12), 5/12. 7. No: the pizzas are different sizes, so the fractions do not refer to the same whole. A quarter of a very large pizza could be more.
Fraction Check: 1. 3/6, because 3 is half of 6 (or 1/2 = (1 × 3)/(2 × 3)). 2. 4/6, 6/9, 8/12. 3. True; a model shows the same area shaded. 4. 4. 5. Examples: 6/10, 9/15, 12/20. 6. 5/12 < 1/2, because 1/2 = 6/12. 7. 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, so 2/3 > 5/8. 8. No: 4/8 = 1/2, because 4 is half of 8; bigger numbers do not mean a bigger fraction.
Scoring tip: give full accuracy credit for any correct equivalent fraction; score reasoning on whether the model or multiplication actually shows why, not on its neatness.
title: Answer key: Equivalent Fractions
